name: Creative Writing With AI Parts Marked
title: Creative Writing With AI Parts Marked
answer: Creative writing with AI parts marked means students may use AI to help draft or spark ideas, but they must show which parts came from the tool, for example by highlighting suggested lines or adding a short note. It matters because the student's own choices, not the machine's, must shape the final piece, and marking AI use keeps that visible and honest.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea addresses the moment in creative writing when students are most tempted to hand the work over to AI, while also recognising that AI can genuinely spark creativity. The approach is not to ban the tool but to keep the student in charge of the final text, so the machine may offer a draft and the student reshapes it. Marking the AI's contribution, through highlighting or a brief note, makes the student's own work visible and turns AI use into an honest part of the writing process. It also connects to the AI use levels described earlier in the book, where a teacher marks what is allowed on each assignment.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a student writing a poem or story might let the tool suggest lines, then revise them, and highlight any lines the tool proposed or add a short note explaining how the tool was used. The book describes this approach through a Finnish poetry study, where the machine offers a draft and the student reshapes it, and through a three month program in Hong Kong in which 82 upper elementary students wrote digital stories about AI. That project shows writing about machines can build both writing skill and AI literacy, helping students think clearly about what machines can and cannot do. The marking practice matches the AI use levels from Chapter 3, where the teacher sets what is allowed on each assignment. The text does not give separate grade band instructions beyond the upper elementary example.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with practice based evidence rather than a formal research claim. It cites the Finnish poetry study at the start of the chapter, where students who revised more wrote better poems (Kangasharju et al., 2022). It also cites a three month program in which 82 upper elementary students in Hong Kong wrote digital stories about AI, and their stories showed real understanding of how AI works (Ng et al., 2022). These findings are reported exactly as the text states them, and no other studies, figures or dates are given.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits set out in the text are that the student's choices, not the machine's, must shape the final piece, and that the AI's contribution should be marked so the student's own work stays visible. Marking can take the form of highlighting suggested lines or adding a short note about how the tool was used. The decision about what is allowed on each assignment stays with the teacher, following the AI use levels from Chapter 3. The text does not set out further restrictions, and nothing here is legal advice.
